items: The “variational EM” formulation is not fully specified: the probabilistic model, latent variables, variational family, and the ELBO or monotonicity guarantees are not clearly defined; the procedure risks being perceived as heuristic alternating training rather than bona fide EM.
It remains unclear how uncertainty is handled or propagated across scales, especially important when one scale (e.g., structure) is predicted (AlphaFold) and potentially noisy.

Key details about datasets, negative sampling, leakage controls, and data preprocessing (e.g., use of predicted vs. experimental structures, homolog filtering, cross-protein family splits) are missing or under-specified.

Comparisons omit several strong modern baselines (e.g., models using protein language model embeddings, large-scale heterogeneous graph link predictors, gradient-balanced multi-task training methods like GradNorm/PCGrad/MGDA).
Robustness analyses are limited: performance under missing/inaccurate structures, cold-start entities (new proteins or drugs), or domain shift is not reported.
Loss functions, optimization schedule, and the specific mapping of E- and M-steps to modules and parameters are insufficiently detailed to reproduce results or scrutinize the EM claim.
Architectural details of the structural encoder and network-level predictor, hyperparameters, and convergence diagnostics are not presented in the provided text.

The manuscript could better contextualize against co-training/co-EM literature, multi-task optimization balancing methods, and recent multi-scale protein modeling approaches (e.g., integrating protein language models with structure and network information).
Discussion of biases and known pitfalls in DDI/PPI datasets (e.g., hub bias, redundancy, dataset construction artifacts) and how the method mitigates them is brief or absent.

Use of features within one year of diagnosis (e.g., NSAID prescriptions) likely captures prodromal symptom management rather than antecedent risk, inflating apparent predictiveness for early diagnosis rather than incident risk.
Median imputation without missingness indicators may bias associations; correlated-feature SHAP attributions can be unstable and misinterpreted without complementary checks.
Model type is binary classification over a fixed horizon; survival analysis or landmarking might better leverage censoring and temporal dynamics.

Calibration metrics (e.g., calibration plots, Brier score), decision-curve analysis, and comparison to strong, simple baselines (e.g., logistic regression with age+sex+BMI) are not reported, limiting assessment of clinical utility.
External validation is temporal but not external in population or health system; generalizability to non-UK settings and non-European ancestries is unclear.
Cluster stability (e.g., bootstrap stability, ARI/NMI across resamples) and rule robustness are not quantified; overlap/coverage–specificity tradeoffs of rules need fuller reporting.
Limited discussion of how class balancing (1:1 matched cases/controls) affects PPV/NPV under real-world prevalence; translational implications of thresholds and recalibration are underexplored.
Omics subset selection and potential sampling bias (age/sex/healthier volunteer bias) are acknowledged but not rigorously characterized.
Survival-model baselines (e.g., RSF or Cox) and explainable survival-to-classification mappings, as explored in recent EHR studies, are not compared.
PRS interpretability/uncertainty and cross-ancestry transportability advances are not engaged; methods such as BRIGHT or uncertainty-aware PRS could contextualize the limited WGPRS value observed.

Multi-label generation is implemented via an arbitrary within-visit ordering (priority order), which can introduce inductive bias and dependence on documentation practices; set-prediction or orderless decoding alternatives are not explored.

Decoding details are under-specified (e.g., teacher forcing vs. free-running during pretraining, end-of-visit termination token, handling the variable number of codes), and potential exposure-bias mitigation is not discussed.
Interpretability is lightly treated; reliance on attention weights as “top indicators” is known to be unstable and insufficient for clinical explanation without additional analyses.

The self-harm cohort description is confusing: the text lists 1,342 cases and 281 controls but also states a 1.9% prevalence among 70,967 PTSD patients; it is unclear which sample is used for model training/evaluation and what the actual class balance is.

Statistical testing uses a one-sided t-test across random seeds; this treats runs as independent samples of the data-generating process and may not accurately capture uncertainty. Better approaches include paired bootstrap or DeLong tests (for AUROC) and bootstrap for AUPRC with per-patient resampling.
Calibration (e.g., reliability curves, Brier score) and decision-analytic metrics (e.g., net benefit/decision curves) are not reported, which are essential for clinical deployment.
External validation is limited (ICU-only MIMIC-IV ICD-10 subset with modest gains); no zero-shot transfer is shown and broader multi-institutional generalization remains unproven.
Important implementation specifics (vocabulary size, ICD code granularity, hierarchy handling, label smoothing, loss formulation for multi-label generation) are missing, limiting reproducibility.
The term “Enformer” is already widely associated with a genomics foundation model; name reuse risks confusion in the literature and searchability.

The paper positions the approach as the first encoder–decoder generative framework for EHR next-visit multi-label prediction; however, subsequent/contemporaneous work (e.g., RAVEN and other next-visit generative EHR foundation models) has closely related objectives and should be discussed and, where possible, compared.

Strong structured baselines beyond LR/LSTM (e.g., LightGBM/TabPFN on ontology-rolled, time-binned counts) often remain competitive on EHR tasks; including such baselines would strengthen empirical claims.
Safety alignment measures are relatively narrow (e.g., blocking package installation) and do not yet constitute a comprehensive, formally verified safety architecture for AFM operation.
The planner–tool interface appears permissive; there is limited evidence of robust precondition checks, formal state machines, or typed parameter contracts to prevent unsafe motion or mode switches.
The optimization objective for PID tuning (SSIM of trace/retrace) may bias toward over-smoothing; no comparative analysis with alternative image-quality or stability metrics is provided.
Only two closed-source LLMs (GPT-4o and GPT-3.5-turbo-0125) are evaluated; there is no comparison to strong open-source models, non-LLM baselines (e.g., rule-based controllers), or human experts.

Statistical reporting is limited: averages are given without confidence intervals, dispersion, or formal significance tests; tool categories with few tasks (e.g., only four for Image Optimizer) are underpowered.
The “multi-agent coordination” degradation indicated in the abstract is not quantified with per-category success rates, ablations, or protocol-level analysis.
Efficiency times appear to emphasize agent/tool reasoning latency rather than end-to-end experimental duration that includes hardware overhead, limiting practical interpretability.
Some claims in the abstract seem stronger than supported by the results (e.g., “struggle even with basic documentation retrieval” versus reported 92%/72% success).
Terminology around “total errors” vs “error rate” and counts per category could be clarified; the donut labels and text occasionally give mixed signals without denominators.
“Mechanical property measurement” is claimed, but demonstrations mainly show roughness and friction in volts; there is no evidence of calibrated modulus or lateral force in SI units.
Limited discussion of recent autonomous SPM frameworks that use deep learning for defect detection, tip repair, and drift compensation at atomic resolution (Related Work: 2404.11162).
No comparison to multi-objective closed-loop strategies for SPM sampling/parameter selection (e.g., MOBO with physically motivated features; Related Work: 2601.05528).
For friction, there is no reference to recent absolute lateral force calibration workflows that could enable reporting in Newtons and traceable uncertainty (Related Work: 2503.18766).
